context: Current closing price of Royal Caribbean (RCL): $264.20 USD as of 2026-05-13.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a current price around 264–265, with very gradual appreciation over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 265.5 essentially assumes continuity — overnight sessions and the next trading day are unlikely to produce dramatic moves absent a major catalyst, so the forecast is anchored tightly to recent price action. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 267, incorporating a mild positive drift assumption consistent with broad equity market tendencies over short horizons. At the one-month horizon, the 270 estimate reflects a somewhat more optimistic view that, absent shocks, the underlying instrument — likely a broad market ETF or index — continues its gradual upward trend, consistent with historical average monthly returns in the low single-digit percentage range.

The confidence interval widths grow in a manner consistent with the square-root-of-time scaling that characterizes random walk dynamics in financial markets. At one day, the 90% CI of roughly plus or minus 4.5–5 points reflects typical daily volatility. The one-week interval widens to roughly plus or minus 19 points, and the one-month interval expands to plus or minus 35 points. These widths were calibrated using approximate historical volatility — if the instrument has annualized volatility around 15–18%, those interval widths are roughly consistent with that regime. Any shift in realized volatility, either a compression during low-activity periods or a spike during stress, would make these intervals too wide or too narrow respectively.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise Federal Reserve policy shift, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data (employment, inflation), geopolitical escalation, or a liquidity event in credit markets could produce moves well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. On the upside, a surprisingly dovish policy signal, strong earnings surprises, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could push prices above the upper bounds. The one-month interval is most vulnerable to these tail risks since it spans a full earnings cycle and multiple economic data releases, any one of which could meaningfully reprice the market in either direction beyond the 90% confidence bounds I specified.
